meaning: A double negative meaning "it's not that I don't...". It admits a possibility or feeling in a reserved, indirect way.
connection: Verb ない-form / い-adjective く-form / noun or な-adjective + で + なくもない／なくはない

senses.label: Not entirely unwilling / not impossible
senses.meaning: Says a possibility or willingness is not completely absent. The tone is hesitant and reserved. Often used to agree reluctantly or to state a position softly.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form minus 「い」 + くもない／くはない (「行かなくもない」, 「考えられなくはない」)
examples: Depending on the conditions, I might take it on.
Well, if you put it that way, I could go.
I can sort of understand how he feels.

senses.label: Somewhat / a little
senses.meaning: Says a feeling or quality is present to some degree. Weaker than a direct statement. Often paired with 「気がする」 or 「感じる」.
senses.connection: い-adjective く-form + なくもない / noun or な-adjective + で + なくもない (「高くなくもない」, 「不便でなくはない」)
examples: I kind of feel the price is a bit high.
This outfit is a little flashy, but it suits you.

notes: A double negative is a weak affirmative, so don't read it as a negative: 「彼の気持ちも分からなくもない」 means "I can understand how he feels, to some extent", not "I don't understand". If you miss one 「ない」 when reading or translating, the meaning is completely reversed.
The tone is reluctant and reserved. Answering a superior or a client with 「やらなくもないです」 sounds grudging or even arrogant, and is rude. To accept, say 「喜んで」 or 「承知しました」; to hold back, say 「検討いたします」.
The connection is often got wrong. Verbs take the 「なく」 of the ない-form: ✕「行かないもない」「行くなくもない」 → ○「行かなくもない」. Nouns and na-adjectives need 「で／じゃ」 first: ✕「便利なくもない」 → ○「便利でなくもない」.

「なくもないが／けど」 is usually followed by a contrast, and the second half is what the speaker really wants to say (in 「おいしくなくもないけど、高すぎる」 the point is "too expensive"). When listening, don't hear only the first half and take it as praise.

daily.title: Invited by a friend
daily.description: You don't really want to go, but you leave the door open.
daily.example: Well, if I have time, I might go.

daily.title: Commenting on food
daily.description: You don't want to say it tastes bad, so you hint.
daily.example: I kind of feel it's a little bland.

daily.title: Understanding someone
daily.description: Showing limited sympathy for what someone did.
daily.example: I can sort of see why he's angry.

work.title: Negotiating
work.description: Leaving room for discussion on a client's request.
work.example: If you could extend the deadline, we might be able to handle it.

work.title: Evaluating a plan
work.description: Giving a cautious view on whether a plan is feasible.
work.example: I think this plan isn't impossible to carry out.

etymology: Built from 「なく」 (the continuative form of 「ない」) + the particle 「も」 or 「は」 + 「ない」, forming a double negative. Negating a negative only partly restores the positive, so the tone stays understated.

similar.title: 〜ないものでもない／〜ないでもない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both express "it's not that I don't...". 「ないものでもない／ないでもない」 is more formal and stiff, and is mostly used for conditional willingness (「条件次第で引き受けないものでもない」). 「なくもない」 is more colloquial, and is also common in statements of feeling such as 「気がしなくもない」.

similar.title: 〜ないことはない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「ないことはない」 leans toward an objective, logical "it's not that it can't be done / it's not that there is none" (「急げば間に合わないことはない」), and the degree of affirmation is higher. 「なくもない」 carries a more subjective, reluctant "to some extent" reserve.

formation: Built from 「なく」 (the continuative form of the negative auxiliary 「ない」), the particle 「も」 or 「は」, and a second 「ない」. The second 「ない」 negates the first, so the two negations should cancel out into a plain affirmative. But because the idea is reached by a roundabout route, it only gets back as far as "it's not that there's none at all", a hedged, weak affirmative. 「も」 carries an "also" nuance, suggesting "this is one of the possibilities too", which makes 「なくもない」 sound more indirect and more reluctant. Switching to the contrastive 「は」 gives 「なくはない」, with the sense of "I won't deny this point (but...)", and it is often followed by 「が」 or 「けど」.

meaning: Raises something as the topic to stress "speaking of its ..., it's truly amazing". Usually followed by an exclamation or evaluation.

senses.label: As for its..., it's really...
senses.meaning: Picks out a noun as the topic on purpose. What follows is the speaker's amazement or strong judgment of its degree. Written style, a bit dramatic.
senses.connection: Noun + たるや (common: 「その迫力たるや」, 「その人気たるや」, 「その味たるや」)
examples: Its sheer power was beyond words.
His popularity is something else.
The damage was beyond imagination.

notes: The second clause must be an exclamation of extreme degree or a strong evaluation; a plain fact won't work: ✕「その値段たるや千円だった」 → ○「その値段たるや、目を疑うほどだった」.
It attaches only to nouns, mostly nouns whose degree can be measured, such as 「迫力」「人気」「規模」 after 「その／彼の」. It cannot follow a verb or adjective: ✕「速いたるや」 → ○「その速さたるや」.

Don't confuse it with 「〜たる者」: 「教師たる者、〜べきだ」 means "anyone who is a teacher should..." and goes on to the proper attitude and duty, whereas 「〜たるや」 lifts a thing up to marvel at its degree. Tell them apart by whether 「や」 follows.
This is a literary, slightly exaggerated written expression. In everyday conversation it sounds affected or jokingly theatrical; 「〜といったら」 is more natural in speech.

daily.title: After a concert
daily.description: Telling a friend how electric the show was.
daily.example: The excitement at that show was incredible!

daily.title: Reading a travel essay
daily.description: The author describes the beauty of the scenery dramatically.
daily.example: The beauty of the scenery was simply breathtaking.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting the huge scale of a disaster.
work.example: The losses are said to reach tens of billions of yen.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.example: Its influence is enough to transform the whole industry.

etymology: 「たる」 is the attributive form of the classical copula 「たり」, and 「や」 is a classical particle for topic and exclamation. It is generally thought to have shifted from "one who is ..." to marking a topic with an exclamatory tone.

similar.title: 〜たる
similar.explanation: Same origin (both contain 「たる」, the attributive form of the classical copula 「たり」). 「たる」 modifies a noun and means "as one who is... (as one should be)", dealing with status and expected conduct (「教師たる者」). 「たるや」 lifts the noun up as the topic and is followed by an exclamation about its degree.

similar.title: 〜（こと）といったら
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both mean "when it comes to..., it's really...". 「（こと）といったら」 is colloquial and often follows a nominalized adjective (「寒さといったら」), and the end can be shortened to 「〜といったらない」. 「たるや」 is written-style, more exaggerated and solemn.

similar.title: 〜ときたら
similar.explanation: Both lift a person or thing up as the topic and then comment on it. 「ときたら」 is colloquial and mostly carries dissatisfaction or blame (「うちの息子ときたら」). 「たるや」 mostly expresses amazement, can be praise or criticism, and is written-style.

formation: Built from 「たる」, the attributive form of the classical copula 「たり」 (equivalent to modern 「である」), plus the classical particle 「や」. 「Nたる」 first establishes the noun solemnly as "that thing which is N itself", and 「や」 is generally understood to raise it high as the topic and add an exclamatory pause. This structure of "solemnly lifting up a thing and then pausing" makes the listener expect an extraordinary evaluation to follow, so the second clause is naturally an exclamation about an astonishing degree. Since both elements are classical, the whole phrase has a written, exaggerated feel.

meaning: "It's only worth something if you do it." Stresses that the real point of something lies in that action.

senses.label: Only worth it if you...
senses.meaning: Something only has meaning or value once you actually do the action. Blunt tone with a Kansai flavor. Often used when talking about duty or principles.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + なんぼだ (「売れてなんぼ」, 「使ってなんぼ」, 「勝ってなんぼ」)
examples: Business is all about making money.
Tools are only worth something if you use them.
Pro athletes live in a world where only winning counts.

notes: It means "it only counts if you do it", not "how many times you did it": 「勝ってなんぼ」 means "winning is what counts", not "how many wins". Only the standalone 「なんぼ」 (「これ、なんぼ？」) means the Kansai "how much?".

It has a Kansai flavor, is blunt and direct, and is not used in business writing or in formal situations with superiors or clients. Saying 「商売は儲けてなんぼですから」 to a client sounds money-minded and tactless.
It attaches to the te-form of a verb: ✕「売るなんぼ」「売れたなんぼ」 → ○「売れてなんぼ」.
「てなんぼ」 is itself the conclusion and often ends the sentence as 「〜てなんぼだ」 or 「〜てなんぼの世界」. Unlike 「てこそ」, it can't be followed by a concrete result: ✕「使ってなんぼ便利さが分かる」 → ○「使ってこそ便利さが分かる」.

daily.title: Telling someone not to save things
daily.description: A friend bought nice clothes but never wears them.
daily.example: Clothes are meant to be worn. Why not wear them more?

daily.title: Talking about life
daily.description: An older person encourages young people to try things.
daily.example: When you're young, making mistakes is the whole point.

work.title: Sales meeting
work.description: A manager stresses the importance of sales figures.
work.example: A product only matters if it sells. Let's deliver results in numbers.

etymology: 「なんぼ」 is Kansai dialect for "how much (money)". 「〜てなんぼ」 roughly meant "it's worth something only after you do it", and is generally thought to have extended to "only valuable if done".

similar.title: 〜てこそ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both mean "only if... then...". 「てこそ」 is standard Japanese and is followed by the result or value that follows (「使ってこそ価値がある」). 「てなんぼ」 is colloquial with a Kansai flavor, and is itself the conclusion "that's where the value is", so it can end the sentence on its own.

similar.title: 〜て初めて
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both carry the sense of "only after doing it". 「て初めて」 focuses on time order: only after doing it did one realize or achieve something for the first time (「親になって初めて分かった」). 「てなんぼ」 focuses on value judgment: if you don't do it, it's meaningless.

formation: Built from the verb te-form plus the Kansai dialect word 「なんぼ」 (= 「いくら」, "how much, what it's worth"). The te-form sets the premise here: "having done...". 「なんぼ」 shifts the topic to an estimate of value. Together they literally mean "only once you've done it can we talk about what it's worth", implying "if you don't do it, it's worth nothing", and so the meaning "it only has value if you do it" arises. 「なんぼ」 was originally a merchant's word used in haggling, so the whole expression has a practical, blunt Kansai flavor, and is often used to assert the proper role or principle of something.

meaning: The reality is the exact opposite of what was expected, how something looks, or what was said. Often surprising or ironic.
connection: Noun + とは裏腹に / とは裏腹な + noun

senses.label: Contrary to...
senses.meaning: The reality is the exact opposite of the first part (expectations, looks, words, etc.). Often describes an unexpected result or a gap between surface and truth.
senses.connection: Noun + とは裏腹に (common: 「期待とは裏腹に」, 「言葉とは裏腹に」, 「見た目とは裏腹に」)
examples: Contrary to everyone's expectations, he lost the match.
Despite what she said, she looked very lonely.
Contrary to its appearance, this dish is very spicy.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「とは裏腹な」 modifies the following noun: "... that is the opposite of ...". 「と裏腹に」 without 「は」 is also used.
senses.connection: Noun + とは裏腹な + noun / noun + と裏腹に
examples: Behind the strong sales lies a harsh reality.
Contrary to the government's announcement, prices keep rising.

notes: The two parts must be the "surface (expectation, appearance, words)" and the "reality" of the same thing, exactly opposite. It can't be used to compare two different people or things: ✕「兄とは裏腹に、弟は背が高い」 → ○「兄にひきかえ、弟は背が高い」.
It also can't be used when things are merely "different" rather than "opposite": ✕「予想とは裏腹に、少し寒かった」 (expecting "cold", it was "a bit cold"). Use it for a real contrast such as 「暖かいという予想とは裏腹に、雪が降った」.
The second part is generally a fact that has already occurred, and doesn't take the speaker's will, commands or requests: ✕「期待とは裏腹に、頑張りましょう」.
「裏腹」 is read 「うらはら」; don't read it 「うらばら」 or 「りふく」.

daily.title: Talking about a friend's personality
daily.description: Saying someone's looks don't match their character.
daily.example: Despite his scary face, he's very kind.

daily.title: Talking about the forecast
daily.description: The weather was the opposite of the forecast.
daily.example: Contrary to the forecast, it was nice all day.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Describing a character whose feelings differ from her face.
daily.example: Behind her smile, she was crying inside.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting a market move that went against expectations.
work.example: Contrary to market expectations, stock prices fell sharply.

work.title: Sales analysis
work.example: Despite the strong promotion, sales are stagnating.

etymology: 「裏腹」 literally means "back and belly". Since these are on opposite sides of the body, it is generally thought to have come to mean "exactly opposite".

similar.title: 〜に反して
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both mean "contrary to...". 「に反して」 is more objective, and its first part can be an expectation or also a rule or intention (「規則に反して」 = against the rules). 「とは裏腹に」 is used only for a gap between expectation, appearance or words and reality, and stresses "saying one thing and meaning another, or things going against one's wishes".

similar.title: 〜にひきかえ
similar.explanation: Both express a strong contrast. 「にひきかえ」 compares two different people or things (「兄にひきかえ弟は」). 「とは裏腹に」 speaks of the surface and the reality of the same thing being opposite.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: Both can be used when the result is unexpected. 「にもかかわらず」 is the concessive "in spite of... still", and its first part is usually a fact (「雨にもかかわらず」). In 「とは裏腹に」 the first part is an expectation or appearance, and the two parts are exactly opposite.

formation: Built from 「と」 (marking the thing compared), the contrastive 「は」, the noun 「裏腹」, and the adverbial 「に」. 「裏腹」 literally means "back and belly"; the back and belly are the two opposite sides of one body, so it is a metaphor for "the front and the inside of one thing being exactly opposite". Thus 「AとはB裏腹に」 means "B stands in a back-to-belly opposition to A", which suits gaps within one thing, such as "what one says vs. what one thinks", "appearance vs. inner reality", or "expectation vs. outcome". Before a noun, 「に」 becomes 「な」 (「期待とは裏腹な結果」), and as a predicate you say 「〜と裏腹だ」.

meaning: Gives a typical example: "even ... is like this, so the rest goes without saying". Usually critical.

senses.label: Even...
senses.meaning: Names the person or thing that should do best or is most representative. If even they are like this, others are worse. The second half is usually negative.
senses.connection: Noun (often a person or role) + にしてからが (common: 「社長にしてからが」, 「先生にしてからが」)
examples: Even the president is late for meetings, so there's no way the staff will follow the rules.
Even the experts are divided.
Even parents don't understand how their children feel.

notes: It names "the person who should do best" and the second clause is a negative evaluation, implying that everyone else is worse. Saying 「部長にしてからが守っていない」 to a superior or the other party's face is severe criticism, and very rude.
It is used only for negative content and can't be used for praise: ✕「社長にしてからが毎朝一番に出社する」 → ○「社長でさえ毎朝一番に出社する」.
Don't confuse it with 「〜てから」 ("after..."). Here 「にして」 is the classical form marking status or subject, and 「にしてからが」 as a whole means "even..."; it doesn't express time order.

daily.title: Complaining about house rules
daily.description: A child complains that adults don't follow the rules either.
daily.example: Even Dad is always on his phone, yet I'm the only one who gets scolded.

daily.title: Reading an opinion piece
daily.description: A column criticizes a widespread problem.
daily.example: Even adults don't mind their manners. It's a real problem.

work.title: Criticizing management in a meeting
work.description: Pointing out that the problem starts at the top.
work.example: Even the managers are taking the rules lightly.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: Criticizing the attitude of the government.
work.example: Even the government refuses to admit responsibility.

etymology: 「にして」 is a classical case-particle use marking the subject or role, 「から」 marks a starting point, and 「が」 is a case particle. It is generally thought to mean literally "starting from ... (it's like this)", extended to "even ...".

similar.title: 〜からして
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both give one representative example to say "even this is the case". 「からして」 is more common and can also give the basis for a judgment (「その態度からして」). 「にしてからが」 is more written-style, mostly refers to people, and is used almost only for criticism.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both are "even...". 「さえ」 is the general form and can be praise or criticism (「子どもでさえ知っている」). 「にしてからが」 names the person who should do best, implying "so the others go without saying", and has a strong negative tone.

similar.title: 〜すら
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「すら」 is the written "even..." and stresses that the example given is an extreme one. 「にしてからが」 gives the most representative person or thing, the one who should lead by example.

formation: Built from the classical case particle 「にして」 (equivalent to 「で」 or 「であって」, pointing to status or subject), the starting-point 「から」, and the case particle 「が」. Literally, "starting from the very person who is...": the person who should set the best example is placed as the "starting point", and if even the starting point is like this, those below him naturally go without saying. 「が」 turns the whole phrase into the subject of the sentence, so that person's behavior follows directly. The structure "starting point = highest standard" means it always carries a critical tone of "even the role model fails".

meaning: Uses something as the standard and handles things in line with it: "in accordance with ...; based on ...".
connection: Noun + に準じて / に準じた + noun / に準ずる + noun

senses.label: In accordance with...
senses.meaning: Handles the second part using the first as the standard. Mostly used for rules, systems and procedures. Formal and objective.
senses.connection: Noun + に準じて (「規定に準じて」, 「前例に準じて」)
examples: Travel expenses are paid in accordance with company rules.
This time, too, we'll follow the method used last time.

senses.label: Equivalent to / on a par with
senses.meaning: Not exactly the same, but treated as equal to the first part. Often modifies a noun. 「準ずる」 is also used.
senses.connection: Noun + に準じた／に準ずる + noun (「正社員に準じた待遇」, 「これに準ずるもの」)
examples: Contract employees also receive treatment equivalent to full-time staff.
Please bring your driver's license or an equivalent document.

notes: 「準じて」 means "handle by analogy, by the same standard", not "obey": ✕「交通ルールに準じて運転する」 → ○「交通ルールに従って運転する」「交通ルールを守って運転する」.
The kanji is 「準」 (standard), often miswritten as the homophone 「順」 (order): ✕「規定に順じて」 → ○「規定に準じて」.

「運転免許証またはこれに準ずるもの」 means "a document of equal validity to a driver's license", not "something following the license". If you misread this in application requirements, you may bring the wrong documents.
Both 「準じる」 and 「準ずる」 are acceptable; 「準ずる」 is more common in regulations and laws. In the middle of a sentence it is written 「〜に準じ、」.

daily.title: Signing up for an event
daily.description: Reading the rules in the event guide.
daily.example: The fee is calculated at the adult rate.

daily.title: Reading a notice
daily.description: Seeing a rule on an apartment notice board.
daily.example: Please keep pets in accordance with the building rules.

work.title: HR regulations
work.description: Setting the conditions for temporary staff.
work.example: Leave may be taken on the same basis as full-time employees.

work.title: Legal document
work.description: Handling matters not covered by a contract.
work.example: Matters not specified in this contract shall be handled in accordance with the relevant laws.

work.title: Application instructions
work.example: Submit an ID or an equivalent document.

etymology: 「準」 originally means "level, standard". 「準じる／準ずる」 means "to take as a standard, to treat in line with". It is a する-type verb formed from the kanji word 「準」 + 「ずる」.

similar.title: 〜にのっとって
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both express taking a rule as the basis. 「にのっとって」 means following rules, laws or tradition strictly (「ルールにのっとって」). 「に準じて」 means treating something by analogy with a standard, in the same way, where the thing used as the model may not apply directly in the first place.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「に基づいて」 expresses a basis in facts, data, experience and the like (「調査に基づいて」). 「に準じて」 expresses handling something by analogy with a certain rule, precedent or treatment.

similar.title: 〜に即して
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both mean acting by a certain standard. 「に即して」 stresses fitting the actual situation or facts (「実情に即して」). 「に準じて」 stresses treating something as equal to a certain standard.

formation: Built from 「に」 (marking the reference) plus the te-form of the suru-verb 「準じる／準ずる」. The kanji 「準」 originally means "level, standard", and also "modeled on, next to" (as in 「準優勝」 and 「準会員」). So 「Aに準じてB」 literally means "taking A as the level line and aligning with it to do B", i.e. "with reference to A, by the same standard as A", not A itself. For this reason it can mean both "handle by analogy with the rule" and "equivalent to" (「正社員に準じた待遇」 = treatment equal to a regular employee, though not one). Before a noun, use 「準じた／準ずる＋noun」.

meaning: Says something may happen or be true. Fairly objective; common in news and reports.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form, or noun + の + 可能性がある

senses.label: There's a possibility that...
senses.meaning: Objectively points out that something may happen or be true. More formal and neutral than 「かもしれない」. Works for good and bad things.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + 可能性がある / noun + の可能性がある (also 「可能性もある」)
examples: It may snow tomorrow.
There may also be errors in this data.
There's no possibility that he's the culprit.

senses.label: High or low possibility
senses.meaning: Use 「高い／低い／大きい」 to describe how likely it is. Common in forecasts and analysis.
senses.connection: 〜可能性が + 高い／低い／大きい (「可能性が高い」, 「可能性は低い」)
examples: The economy is likely to recover this year.
At this rate, the chance of success is probably low.

senses.label: Can't be ruled out
senses.meaning: 「可能性は否定できない」 and 「可能性も考えられる」 point out a risk carefully. Cautious and formal.
senses.connection: 〜可能性は否定できない / 〜可能性も考えられる
examples: We can't rule out that the accident was caused by human action.
It could also be due to another cause.

notes: Chinese 可能 can be an adverb, but Japanese 「可能性」 is only a noun: ✕「彼は可能性来る」 → ○「彼は来る可能性がある」「彼は来るかもしれない」.
Don't confuse it with 「可能だ」: 「可能だ」 means "it can be done", while 「可能性がある」 means "it may happen". ✕「予約の変更は可能性があります」 → ○「予約の変更は可能です」. Mixing them up reverses the meaning.
Connection: after a noun add 「の」, and a verb attaches directly: ✕「雨可能性」 → ○「雨の可能性」; ✕「降るの可能性」 → ○「降る可能性」.
Degree is expressed with 「高い／低い／大きい」, not 「多い／少ない」: ✕「可能性が多い」 → ○「可能性が高い」.

daily.title: Weather forecast
daily.description: A presenter explains the chance of rain.
daily.example: Rain is possible from the afternoon.

daily.title: Meeting a friend
daily.description: Warning that you might be late.
daily.example: The trains are delayed, so I might be a bit late.

work.title: Risk report
work.description: Reporting a project risk to your boss.
work.example: We may not meet the deadline.

work.title: News report
work.example: Police believe it is highly likely that several people were involved in the incident.

work.title: Academic paper
work.example: The possibility that this result is due to differences in measurement methods cannot be ruled out.

etymology: 「可能性」 is a kanji compound meaning "possibility". Combined with 「がある」, it literally means "a possibility exists".

similar.title: 〜おそれがある
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both point out objectively what may happen. 「おそれがある」 is used only for fear that something bad will happen (「台風が上陸するおそれがある」). 「可能性がある」 can be used for good or bad things and is more neutral.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「かもしれない」 is the speaker's subjective guess and is common in speech. 「可能性がある」 is more objective and formal, can be quantified with 「高い／低い」, and is common in reports and news.

similar.title: 〜かねない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both can express that some result may occur. 「かねない」 is used only for bad results and carries the speaker's worry or criticism (「事故になりかねない」). 「可能性がある」 is calm and neutral in tone.

formation: Built from the Sino-Japanese noun 「可能性」 (可 = can, 能 = be able to do, 性 = quality, i.e. "the quality of being able to become real"), the particle 「が」 marking the thing that exists, and the existence verb 「ある」. The structure is the same as 「時間がある」 or 「問題がある」, literally "a possibility exists". Since the core is a noun, it can be modified by a preceding clause (「雪が降る可能性」), measured with 「高い／低い／大きい」, and its predicate can be swapped for 「否定できない」 or 「考えられる」. This construction of "talking about possibility as something measurable" makes it more objective than 「かもしれない」 and suited to analysis and reporting. Changing 「ある」 to 「ない」 means "there is no possibility".

meaning: "Assuming / treating as ... (and acting on it)": handling what follows on a given premise.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form, or noun + である + ものとして

senses.label: Assuming that...
senses.meaning: Temporarily assumes the first part is true and thinks or acts on that basis. It need not be a fact. Common in explanations, plans and calculations.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + ものとして (「〜ものとして考える」, 「〜ものとして計算する」)
examples: We booked the venue assuming everyone would attend.
Please calculate on the assumption that the company covers the costs.

senses.label: Treated as / deemed to be
senses.meaning: Treats the first part as an established fact: "deemed ...". Common in formal rules and notices.
senses.connection: Verb plain form (often negative or た-form) + ものとして扱う／みなす
examples: If we don't hear from you by the deadline, you will be treated as absent.
Please forget this matter as if it never happened.

notes: The notice 「期限までに返事がない場合は、欠席するものとして扱います」 is a rule that "no reply means you are deemed absent". Don't skip over it when you read it, or you will be handled as absent automatically.
「この話はなかったものとしてください」 means "please treat this matter as if it never happened". In business it amounts to cancelling an agreement and is heavy in tone, so don't say it casually to clients or superiors.
Don't confuse it with the status-marking 「〜として」: 「学生として参加する」 means "take part as a student", while 「学生であるものとして扱う」 means "treat as a student (regardless of the facts)". A noun needs 「である」: ✕「学生ものとして」.
「ものとしては」, as in 「子ども向けのものとしては」, means "as a thing of..." and isn't the assumption meaning.

daily.title: Sulking with a friend
daily.description: Saying you'll treat something as if it never happened.
daily.example: I'll pretend I didn't hear what you just said.

daily.title: Planning a trip
daily.example: Let's assume it will rain and plan some indoor activities too.

work.title: Meeting notice
work.description: Explaining how no reply will be handled.
work.example: If we don't hear from you, we will proceed on the assumption that you will attend.

work.title: Project budget
work.description: Making an estimate under an assumed condition.
work.example: The estimate assumed an exchange rate of 150 yen to the dollar.

etymology: 「もの」 is a formal noun, and 「として」 marks a role or standpoint. Together they literally mean "(treating) as such a thing", which gives the sense of assuming or deeming.

similar.title: 〜ものとする
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built from 「もの」 plus 「とする」). 「ものとする」 is used at the end of laws and contracts to express a stipulation or interpretation (「〜は無効とするものとする」). 「ものとして」 is a pause form followed by a concrete action (「〜ものとして計算する」).

similar.title: 〜としたら・〜とすれば
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both express assumption. 「としたら／とすれば」 means "if..." and is followed by an inference or judgment. 「ものとして」 means "treat as holding for now" and is followed by the action taken on that basis, and can also mean "deemed an established fact".

similar.title: 〜を前提に／〜を前提として
similar.explanation: Similar meaning; both take a certain condition as the basis. 「を前提に」 attaches to a noun and states plainly "with... as the precondition". 「ものとして」 attaches to a clause and means handling things by assuming or deeming it so for the time being.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: Same origin (both contain 「として」). 「noun＋として」 expresses status, qualification or standpoint (「代表として」). 「ものとして」 follows a clause and expresses assumption or deeming.

formation: Built from the formal noun 「もの」, the particle 「と」 of recognition, and 「して」, the te-form of 「する」. 「Xとする」 originally means "to set as X, to treat as X"; with 「もの」 added in front to nominalize the clause, 「〜ものとする」 means "to treat (something) as being the case". The te-form 「して」 makes a pause, and what follows is an action taken on that basis: "first treat it as so, then do...". Because this is a "stipulation" and not a "fact", the first part can be a tentative assumption or a prescriptive "deemed", which is why it can be used both in plans and calculations and in regulations.
